scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4618: Office/Principle department PCs (192.168.3.0/24) report
they cannot reach the Internet Lab (128.168.0.x) -- the external-facing lab
segment has been unreachable all morning. The Office team believes the WAN/uplink
between the routers that carries traffic toward 128.168.0.0/16 went down. Please
find and confirm the fault, and tell us which link or device to bring back up.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The inter-router links are up, RIP is converged,
  and the 128.168.0.0/16 (Internet Lab) prefix is reachable from the Office segment;
  Office hosts reach 128.168.0.x with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a downed WAN/uplink that is not actually down.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- Office (192.168.3.x) cannot
reach the Internet Lab (128.168.0.x) -- is NOT reproducible: an Office host reaches
128.168.0.x with 0% loss, the inter-router links carrying traffic toward
128.168.0.0/16 are up, ripd is running on router0/router1/router2, and the
128.168.0.0/16 prefix is present in the RIP tables.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path to the Internet Lab is healthy
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the Office ->
Internet Lab path, finds it working, verifies the inter-router link state and the
128.168.0.0/16 route, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a downed WAN/uplink
to satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
No outage is present now. Office/Principle hosts can reach the Internet Lab over the R1–R2 WAN, and the link is healthy. From office_pc (192.168.3.2), pings to 128.168.0.2/.3/.4/.5 all succeed (0% loss). A traceroute from office_pc to 128.168.0.2 shows the expected path: 192.168.3.1 (router1) -> 20.20.0.2 (router2) -> 128.168.0.2. On router1, the route to 128.168.0.0/16 is installed via 20.20.0.2 on eth3 (RIP learned). On router2, the reverse routes to 192.168.3.0/24 and 192.168.4.0/24 are present via 20.20.0.1 on eth2 (RIP learned). Physical link checks confirm the inter-router WAN is up: ethtool shows “Link detected: yes” on router1 eth3 (20.20.0.1/8) and router2 eth2 (20.20.0.2/8), and interface stats show traffic with zero errors/drops. 

Affected component: none currently. 
Mechanism: Bidirectional routing is present via RIP, and data plane forwarding across R1–R2 is operational. 
Localization: WAN between router1 eth3 and router2 eth2 (20.20.0.0/8) verified up; LAN gateways 192.168.3.1 and 192.168.4.1 are reachable. 
Root cause: Not reproducible; no evidence of a current WAN or routing fault. 
Corrective fix: No action required now. If the morning issue was intermittent, enable interface/RIP logging on router1/2 and monitor the R1–R2 link (eth3/eth2) for flaps; consider SNMP/telemetry alerts to capture future transient events.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly confirms the R1–R2 link is up (link detected, no errors) and shows Office pings/traceroute to 128.168.0.0/16 succeeding with the route present in RIP.

Agent's ping and traceroute tests directly demonstrate Office -> Internet Lab connectivity; router interface and routing command outputs (though truncated) plus interface statistics support the assertion of healthy links and RIP-learned routes. Minor unshown snippets (exact route line or explicit 'Link detected: yes') are implied by the visible evidence but do not undermine the conclusion.
